newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa reserves edge up, helped by bond proceeds.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa reserves edge up, helped by bond proceeds.

text.p: South Africa's sinking gold and foreign exchange reserves edged up in October, despite central bank sales of dollars to support the ailing rand, figures released on Thursday showed.
The Reserve Bank said reserves rose by 241.5 million rand ($51.4 million) in October to 10.28 billion, even though foreign credit lines of 612 million were repaid in the month.
Economists said the increase was mainly due to proceeds from the government's foreign bond issues. Market analysts had expected a fall to about 9.6 billion rand.

Equisec economist Dawie Roodt said if proceeds of the $300 million Yankee bond issue were not included, the central bank would be left with net reserves of roughly 8.8 billion rand, lower than the net reserves of about 9.4 billion in September.
Reserves also got a boost from a higher rand gold price, which lifted gold's contribution to 60 percent of total gross reserves.
In dollar terms, reserves still dipped marginally and economists said the position remained critical with official holdings of gold and foreign currencies only enough to cover four weeks of imports.

At prevailing month-end exchange rates, October's reserves amounted to $2.17 billion, down from $2.22 billion in September, and the lowest level since early 1994 when confidence was hit by political fears in the run-up to elections.
By end-1995, reserves surged back to $4.4 billion as post-apartheid South Africa sucked in increasing foreign investment -- but the run on the rand which started in February 1996 sent them tumbling.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said earlier this week that low reserves were the biggest single problem facing South Africa at present.
The authorities have come under mounting pressure to take action to abolish foreign exchange controls but Stals said such calls were unreasonable given the precariously low level of reserves.

Optimists argue that the scrapping of foreign exchange controls on residents would send a clear signal of the government's confidence in the economy and encourage foreign investors to return to the country.

Speculative selling spurred by concerns over structural problems in the South African economy sent the rand tumbling to an all-time low of 4.77 against the dollar last week. But it has since recovered to around 4.70.
